title: Top U.S. Health Official Backed a Medication Policy Shift That Benefited a Company She Has Stock In
author: Brandon Roberts
content:
Last November, the Department of Health and Human Services announced the
elimination of “black box” warnings on hormone replacement therapies, aiming
to reverse nearly two decades of stigma surrounding a key treatment for
menopause symptoms.  

Among the officials at a [press
conference](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rtvhshHADM0&t=1030s) about the
decision was Alicia Jackson, director of a federal health agency that invests
taxpayer money in medical technology and research. As Jackson stood behind a
lectern adorned with the HHS logo, she praised the new policy, calling it a
victory for women and science.

“Today we have the opportunity to add up to a decade of healthy years to the
life of every woman that you love,” Jackson said. “The science is clear:
Hormone therapy is safe and effective. And it is hugely beneficial to the vast
majority of women.”

Less clear that day were the financial benefits the new policy could bring
Jackson, according to disclosure records obtained by ProPublica.  

Jackson is the founder and former chief executive of
[Evernow](https://www.evernow.com/), an online platform that connects women
with medical experts who treat the symptoms of menopause. Although she left
for federal service last year, she kept at least $115,000 in Evernow stock and
an unknown amount of stock options, [records
show](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-team-financial-
disclosures/appointees/jackson-alicia/#6_9086_20).

Those are just part of a multimillion-dollar portfolio Jackson holds with her
husband, a venture capitalist, that poses potential conflicts of interest with
her work overseeing the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, known as
ARPA-H.

It’s unclear what role, if any, Jackson played in dropping the black box
warning, the most serious type of federal safety warning that is reserved for
drugs with severe side effects or life-threatening risks. A different agency,
the Food and Drug Administration, regulates drugs, and its panel of experts
had recommended an end to the warning requirement months before Jackson
arrived in government.

But ethics experts called Jackson’s official endorsement of the warning
removal “alarming” and an “obvious conflict of interest,” noting federal law
prohibits government employees from participating “personally and
substantially” in matters that could influence their personal finances — even
making statements at a press conference or in a news release, [as she also
did](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/hhs-advances-womens-
health-removes-misleading-fda-warnings-hormone-replacement-therapy).

“We should care because her company is apparently intending to profit off this
change in policy that she endorsed as a government official while still
retaining a financial interest in the company,” said Virginia Canter, who
served as an ethics lawyer at the White House, Treasury Department and
Securities and Exchange Commission during the presidencies of George H.W.
Bush, Bill Clinton, George W. Bush and Barack Obama.

“I say it puts her within the zone of a potential violation,” she said.  

Months after the announced end to the warning notices, Evernow [launched a
nationwide expansion](https://www.freep.com/press-
release/story/175412/evernow-expands-telehealth-access-for-menopause-care-
across-the-u-s/).

Under federal law, agency officials like Jackson are required to submit
financial disclosure forms, which must then be certified as complying with
ethics laws. But Jackson’s two financial disclosures — filed last October and
two months ago — remain uncertified. Canter said it is not unusual for an
agency’s ethics office to ask the inspector general to investigate if staff
cannot certify that an individual’s disclosure forms meet ethics standards.  

Over two months, ProPublica sought comment from Jackson and submitted
questions about her work, investments and ethics records. Jackson did not
respond, and HHS never addressed our detailed questions.

But in a statement to ProPublica last week, an agency spokesperson said
Jackson has been placed on administrative leave and HHS would “assess the
facts before determining any change in her status. HHS requires all officials
to comply with federal ethics laws, regulations, and policies.”

HHS declined to answer additional questions about the reasons for Jackson’s
leave, the decision’s timing or whether the inspector general was
investigating.

Earlier this week, [Bloomberg Law
reported](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/health-law-and-business/health-
research-agency-head-on-administrative-leave-hhs-says) on the HHS statement
that Jackson was on leave and made public a [draft memo by one of the agency’s
senior officials](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28849718-bm8c/) that
would have granted Jackson a conflict waiver involving many of her and her
husband’s extensive investments. Since she joined ARPA-H, the memo said,
Jackson and her husband’s financial ties required her to recuse herself from
“a significant portion” of her duties, including discussions about funding
awarded by her agency. The waiver named 30 investments and would have allowed
Jackson to take part in decisions that could affect those interests. Evernow
is not listed.

Bloomberg reported that two firms with ties to Jackson sought ARPA-H funding,
but it was unclear if either received any. HHS did not respond to ProPublica’s
questions asking whether the waiver was ever granted or if the firms had
received money from ARPA-H. The Office of Government Ethics does not list
Jackson among federal officials who have received waivers.

Jackson’s disclosures are among 2,400 added Thursday to [ProPublica’s Trump
Team Financials database](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-team-
financial-disclosures/), a searchable tool launched in March. The records
detail the finances of more than 2,300 officials appointed by President Donald
Trump. Since last year, we’ve requested disclosure records from 127 federal
agencies and the White House. Disclosures from roughly 1,500 appointees remain
unreleased.

The Trump administration’s massive cuts to the federal bureaucracy have taken
a toll on the ranks of ethics staff. By the end of 2025, there were 274 fewer
full-time ethics officials, according [to a recent
analysis](https://campaignlegal.org/update/documented-decline-ethics-and-
accountability-federal-agencies) of federal survey records by the government
watchdog group Campaign Legal Center. Some agencies said the losses hampered
ethics officers’ ability to conduct training and monitor employee compliance.

Trump appointees failed to file nearly 420 legally mandated public financial
disclosure reports last year, almost a fourfold spike compared with the Biden
administration’s last full year, the center found. Nevertheless, our database
provides the most complete source yet for this administration’s ethics
documents.

### Potential Serious Conflicts

Jackson spent years navigating the worlds of technological research,
government and entrepreneurship, according to her [government
bio](https://arpa-h.gov/about/people/alicia-jackson) and [LinkedIn
profile](https://www.linkedin.com/in/alicia-jackson/).

After earning a doctorate in materials science from the Massachusetts
Institute of Technology in 2007, she worked briefly as a U.S. Senate policy
staffer. She subsequently joined the Pentagon’s Defense Advanced Research
Projects Agency as a program manager, later becoming deputy director of its
first biotechnology office.

Jackson left the Defense Department in mid-2015, going on to lead several
biotech businesses before starting Evernow in 2019. The San Francisco-based
company connects women experiencing sometimes debilitating menopause symptoms
with medical providers who prescribe treatments.

Evernow offers patients one-time treatments or memberships for frequent care.
Its website lists celebrity angel investors, including Gwyneth Paltrow,
Cameron Diaz, Demi Moore and Drew Barrymore.

Jackson was [appointed by Trump as ARPA-H’s second
director](https://arpa-h.gov/about/people/alicia-jackson) and was sworn in on
Oct. 20, 2025. The agency, created three years earlier to spur revolutionary
biomedical research and technologies, has a $1.5 billion budget. It has issued
numerous contracts and grants, including $160 million for genetic medicines
combating rare diseases and $144 million to study existing treatments for age-
related illnesses.

In both of her financial statements, Jackson said she owned Evernow stock
worth between $115,002 and $300,000. (Federal disclosures include value
ranges, not specific figures.) She also listed company stock options whose
value, she said in her most recent financial report, were “not readily
ascertainable.” (In a statement late Wednesday, Evernow said Jackson does not
currently hold a financial interest in the company. The firm did not
immediately respond to follow-up questions.)

[Jackson’s disclosures](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-team-financial-
disclosures/appointees/jackson-alicia/#6_9086_23) also show investments in
Gameto Inc., a Texas-based biotechnology company working through a two-year,
$10 million award from ARPA-H to create ovarian treatments preventing
menopause-related diseases. The award predated Jackson joining ARPA-H. But as
her office oversaw Gameto’s project, her stock’s value increased, documents
show.

Jackson’s Gameto investment was worth between $15,001 and $50,000 in her
October 2025 disclosure. Her Aug. 13 filing shows it grew to between $50,001
and $100,000. It’s unclear what drove the increase in value.

In addition, Jackson owns more than 60 venture capital and private equity
funds that she says do not disclose their holdings to investors.

These include at least 13 funds managed by 137 Ventures, a venture capital
firm co-founded by Jackson’s husband, Alex Jacobson. The company invests in a
wide range of industries, including healthcare, digital health and medical
device companies, according to its website.

Federal appointees must list their spouses’ employment, but Jackson never
included her [husband’s role](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jacobsonalex/) at
[137 Ventures](https://www.137ventures.com/team) on her public disclosures.
Jacobson did not respond to requests for comment.

Ethics experts said Jackson’s funds could pose a serious conflict of interest
if the underlying businesses they invested in received grants or contracts
from her agency. To resolve such risks, federal agencies typically require
employees to work with the investment vehicles to identify the contents of
such funds. If the investment firms insisted on anonymity, employees could be
required to sell the funds or recuse themselves from actions potentially
affecting the assets, the experts said.

However, 10 months after starting work at HHS, Jackson retained the funds and
their underlying investments remained undisclosed, according to her August
financial statement.

Kedric Payne, Campaign Legal Center’s vice president, general counsel and
senior director for ethics, said Jackson’s lack of disclosure about her
husband and the funds she owns “suggests that agency leaders may be hiding
their conflicts of interest from the public, and there is no ethics
enforcement to stop it.”

The disclosures also show her husband owns between $5 million and $25 million
worth of stock in Palantir Technologies, which had a [$19 million
contract](https://www.usaspending.gov/award/CONT_AWD_75N95024F00003_7529_75N95023D00027_7529)
from Jackson’s agency when she became ARPA-H director. Palantir, which has
similar contracts with other federal agencies, is using its software and AI
technology to build and improve ARPA-H’s data infrastructure and operational
systems. In June, ARPA-H extended the company’s contract by a year, records
show. [The
renewal](https://www.usaspending.gov/award/CONT_AWD_75N99226F00002_7529_47QTCA24D004L_4732)
is worth up to $13.7 million for Palantir.

The draft waiver obtained by Bloomberg would have allowed Jackson to take part
in decisions that could affect Palantir, Gameto and more than two dozen other
investments but says she must still comply with the terms of an ethics
agreement. The draft waiver includes a note dated April 30 — six months after
Jackson started the job — that says discussions about the ethics agreement
were ongoing. In addition to Evernow, the waiver does not specifically mention
the funds managed by 137 Ventures.

HHS officials would not answer repeated questions about whether Jackson
recused herself from Palantir’s contract, has an ethics agreement or has
divested any assets. The agency has not produced an ethics agreement in
response to a July Freedom of Information Act request.

### Public Good or Personal Gain?

Since January 2025, ProPublica has continually obtained disclosure records to
investigate how personal financial interests have intersected with government
decision-making inside the Trump administration. The new disclosures added to
our searchable tool Thursday include many that have raised concerns about
additional conflicts of interest, including at HHS.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Jackson’s ultimate boss, has drawn
questions about whether he used his office to help his wife, actress Cheryl
Hines.

![An out-of-focus man in a suit and tie sits at a table in the foreground
while adjusting a microphone during a Senate hearing. A woman in a business
suit is in focus just behind him and is surrounded by many
people.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/GettyImages-2196609300.jpg?w=2560)Cheryl Hines, wife
of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., watches her husband testify during
his Senate Finance Committee confirmation in 2025. Anna Moneymaker/Getty
Images

According to his latest financial disclosure, Hines’ media company, Youngster
Productions Inc., [received $210,000](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-
team-financial-disclosures/appointees/kennedy-jr-robert-f/#5_9108_1.10) in
consulting fees from [MAHA Action](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-team-
financial-disclosures/search/?q=MAHA+Action), a nonprofit promoting Kennedy’s
Make America Healthy Again agenda. Under the contract, Hines has vigorously
advocated for MAHA Action, appearing in several videos and press releases. The
group has also claimed credit for policy actions launched by Kennedy’s HHS.

News of the contract, first [reported by The New York
Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/23/us/politics/rfk-jr-book-advances-
maha.html), prompted the Campaign Legal Center to ask the HHS inspector
general to examine whether Kennedy made or influenced policies that benefited
his wife. Kennedy also received [more than $270,000 in
gifts](http://projects.propublica.org/trump-team-financial-
disclosures/appointees/kennedy-jr-robert-f/#dsid-9) from allies working to
bolster MAHA, his disclosure showed.

“Americans deserve to know whether their leaders are prioritizing the public
good or focusing more on their personal financial gain,” said Payne of
Campaign Legal Center.

HHS denied any wrongdoing by Kennedy, telling the Times the secretary
“complies with all applicable federal ethics laws, regulations and financial
disclosure requirements.”

Campaign Legal Center’s analysis of federal ethics staff this year found
Kennedy’s cuts to the agency eliminated nearly 30% of HHS’ full-time ethics
workers.

Another HHS official whose disclosures raised ethical alarms was the agency’s
top attorney, Mike Stuart. Stuart was reassigned after a [Washington Sun
investigation](https://www.washingtonsun.com/money/hhs-official-stock-trading-
oge?redirected=notus_org) found he invested in a company doing business with
the department and repurchased stock in other businesses that ethics officials
had required him to sell.

The Office of Government Ethics refused to certify [Stuart’s annual disclosure
report](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-team-financial-
disclosures/appointees/stuart-michael/) “due to continued non-compliance” with
his [ethics
agreement](https://static.notus.org/0e/00/373513da4fca930212bfc20e2832/stuart-
michael-finalea.pdf), the Sun revealed.

Stuart said he didn’t know of the company’s involvement with the department
and immediately sold his stock when ethics officials raised questions. “My
whole career, I’ve never had even a whiff of an ethical issue. I’m extra
careful that I am completely in compliance,” Stuart told the Sun.

The disclosures obtained by ProPublica since early last year have revealed
potential conflicts across the federal government, including at the highest
levels.

In December, ProPublica reported that Trump had appointed more than 200 people
who collectively owned — personally or with their spouses — between $175
million and $340 million in cryptocurrency investments at the time they filed
their disclosures. Some hold [positions overseeing or influencing crypto
industry regulation](https://www.propublica.org/article/todd-blanche-crypto-
doj-trump).

Among them is Todd Blanche, Trump’s former criminal defense attorney and now
the nation’s attorney general. [Blanche’s
disclosures](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-team-financial-
disclosures/appointees/blanche-todd/) show that he [owned at least
$159,000](https://www.propublica.org/article/todd-blanche-crypto-doj-trump) in
crypto-related assets last year when, as the Justice Department’s second-
highest official, [he shut
down](https://www.justice.gov/dag/media/1395781/dl?inline) investigations into
crypto companies, dealers and exchanges.

Democrats in Congress [accused
Blanche](https://www.propublica.org/article/todd-blanche-crypto-conflict-
senator-letter) of a “glaring conflict of interest”; a Justice Department
spokesperson said Blanche’s action was “appropriately flagged, addressed and
cleared in advance.” An Office of Government Ethics official noted on
Blanche’s latest disclosure that the inspector general “declined further
action” related to the crypto holdings.

![A man in a dark suit and red tie speaks with a woman in a plaid jacket who
is holding her bottom lip during an event at the White
House.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/GettyImages-2255818573.jpg?w=2560)Former U.S. Attorney
General Pam Bondi speaks with Todd Blanche, then her deputy and now attorney
general, in the White House in January. Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images

Other disclosures helped show that senior executive branch officials,
[including Pam Bondi](https://www.propublica.org/article/pam-bondi-trump-
media-stock-tariffs) when she was attorney general, made well-timed securities
trades, [selling stocks just before markets
plunged](https://www.propublica.org/article/us-officials-stock-sales-trump-
tariffs) because Trump announced new tariffs. (The officials either did not
respond to requests for comment or denied having insider information before
trading.)

Disclosure forms also revealed in July that [Federal Communications Commission
officials](https://www.propublica.org/article/paramount-mergers-fcc-kennedy-
center-gala) took pricey gifts from Paramount, including tickets worth
[$12,000](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-team-financial-
disclosures/appointees/trusty-olivia/) and [skybox
seats](https://www.propublica.org/article/fcc-paramount-gifts-brendan-carr-
ethics-complaint-warner-bros-merger) worth
[$125,000](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-team-financial-
disclosures/appointees/carr-brendan/) each for the annual honors gala at the
Kennedy Center. The media giant provided the perks while seeking FCC approval
for its mergers with Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery. (The FCC said agency
ethics officers approved the commissioners’ attendance as consistent with
ethics law.)

Our database has helped other news organizations uncover potential conflicts
of interest. [The Lever](https://www.levernews.com/), for instance, [found
that the Pentagon’s chief technology officer](https://www.levernews.com/the-
pentagons-ai-gatekeeper-holds-stock-in-anthropics-rival/) was “a central
figure in the decision to blacklist the AI company Anthropic” while owning a
stake in a competitive AI developer. A Defense Department spokesperson said
the official, Emil Michael, fully complied with ethics requirements.

Benefited a Company She Has Stock In](https://www.propublica.org/article/hhs-
alicia-jackson-menopause-treatment-policy) appeared first on
[ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
